issues.legal_issue: A competent legislature may enact a retrospective law that changes the legal basis of a levy invalidated by a court without impermissibly overruling the court’s judgment.
material_facts: Earlier decisions held that the State legislatures lacked competence to levy the disputed cesses and taxes on minerals.
Parliament enacted provisions creating those levies retrospectively, relying on its own legislative competence over the subject.
The earlier judgments did not hold that Parliament lacked power to impose the levies.
issues.conclusion: The validation law did not annul or overrule the earlier judgments; Parliament validly changed the basis on which the levies were imposed.
issues.legal_principle: Under the separation of powers, a legislature cannot exercise judicial power by merely declaring a court’s decision ineffective. It may, however, alter the law or the basis of the decision, consistently with constitutional limits, so that the decision could not have been given in the altered circumstances. The Court applied Shri Prithvi Cotton Mills v. Broach Borough Municipality and distinguished Madan Mohan Pathak v. Union of India and A.V. Nachane v. Union of India, which it considered factually inapposite.

predicates.validation_statute_challenge: The proceeding challenges a law enacted to validate a levy previously held invalid by a court.
predicates.enacting_legislature_competent: The legislature enacting the new law has authority to legislate on the subject of the levy.
predicates.legal_basis_changed: The new law itself changes the legal basis of the levy rather than merely declaring the earlier court decision ineffective.

issues.definition: When a challenge to a validating law concerns a levy within the enacting legislature’s authority, and the law changes the basis of the earlier decision, the law may operate despite that decision.

issues.legal_issue: A parliamentary deeming provision incorporating earlier State levy provisions can itself create those levies retrospectively.
material_facts: The validation law deemed provisions in scheduled State enactments relating to mineral cesses and taxes to have been enacted by Parliament.
The earlier State provisions contained the terms creating the levies.
The validation law deemed those provisions to have remained in force for a specified past period.
issues.conclusion: The deeming provision was sufficient to create the levies retrospectively; Parliament was not required to enact a separate provision expressly imposing each levy before giving it retrospective effect.
issues.legal_principle: A validating law is not required to follow a fixed verbal formula if its language achieves its purpose. The Court relied on Krishnachandra Gangopadhyaya v. Union of India, which upheld materially similar deeming language, and considered the approach in Joara Sugar Mills v. State of Madhya Pradesh and the Sugarcane Cess (Validation) Act, 1961.

predicates.validation_statute_challenge: The proceeding challenges a law enacted to validate a levy previously held invalid by a court.
predicates.parliament_adopted_existing_levy_terms: Parliament incorporated provisions that set out the terms of the previously imposed levy.
predicates.deeming_language_makes_them_parliamentar: The law deems the incorporated provisions to have been enacted by Parliament for the relevant past period.

issues.definition: In a challenge to a validating law, incorporating earlier levy terms and deeming them parliamentary law for a past period creates the levy for that period.

issues.legal_issue: A retrospective validation of a levy permits collection of amounts due but not collected during the validated period.
material_facts: The law deemed the relevant levy provisions to have been enacted by Parliament for the validated period.
Some amounts due under those provisions had not been collected by the end of that period.
The law validated the levy and related actions, and did not limit its effect to amounts already collected.
issues.conclusion: Amounts due but not collected during the validated period could be collected after that period.
issues.legal_principle: Once the levy is validly created retrospectively, there is no principled distinction between amounts already collected and amounts that remain unpaid. The Court read the validation and collection provisions as validating the imposition as well as collection, and rejected the argument that the absence of an express recovery clause confined the law to preserving past collections.

predicates.validation_statute_challenge: The proceeding challenges a law enacted to validate a levy previously held invalid by a court.
predicates.retrospective_levy_created: The law creates the levy for a past period by giving legal effect to the levy terms for that period.
predicates.amount_remained_unpaid: An amount due under the levy for the validated period had not been collected.

issues.definition: When a validating law creates a levy retrospectively, an amount due under it but left unpaid remains recoverable.

issues.legal_issue: Parliament may impose different rates in different States when those rates preserve historically existing State rates in a validating law.
material_facts: The scheduled State enactments had imposed different rates in different States.
Parliament’s validation law adopted those existing rates while responding to judgments invalidating the State levies.
The challenge was to legislative competence and the levies, not to the historical differences in rates.
issues.conclusion: The different rates were not discriminatory in the circumstances and did not violate Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Parliament may legislate for only part of the country and may prescribe different rates in different States where the distinction is reasonable and justified. The Court relied on State of Madras v. N.K. Nataraj Mudaliar and the reasoning in King v. Barger, and held that preserving the pre-existing rates supplied a historical justification in this context.

predicates.validation_statute_challenge: The proceeding challenges a law enacted to validate a levy previously held invalid by a court.
predicates.prior_state_rates_differed: The relevant State laws had imposed different rates of the levy in different States before the validating law was enacted.
predicates.parliament_preserved_historical_rates: The validating law retained those earlier State rates rather than creating new differences between States.

issues.definition: When a validating law preserves rate differences that already existed under State laws, those differences are not discriminatory merely because the parliamentary law applies them across States.

issues.legal_issue: Parliament need not make a fresh declaration of Union control each time it imposes or changes a mineral tax after the States have been wholly denuded of power to tax minerals.
material_facts: The existing parliamentary declaration had placed regulation of mines and mineral development under Union control to the extent provided by the relevant legislation.
Earlier decisions held that the declaration and legislation had wholly deprived the States of power to tax minerals.
The validation law imposed the levies through Parliament rather than restoring State taxing power.
issues.conclusion: No fresh declaration was required for Parliament to enact the levies; the States’ denudation of power was total, not partial.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Entry 54 of List I, Entry 50 of List II, section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, and the holdings in India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu and Orissa Cement Ltd. v. State of Orissa that the States were wholly denuded of power to tax minerals while the declaration remained in force.

predicates.mineral_tax_legislation_challenge: The proceeding challenges legislation imposing a tax on minerals.
predicates.existing_union_control_declaration: A parliamentary law has already placed the relevant regulation and development of minerals under Union control.
predicates.states_wholly_lack_taxing_power: The States have no remaining power to impose the mineral tax while that Union-control arrangement remains in force.

issues.definition: Where mineral taxation is challenged after Union control has already left the States without taxing power, Parliament does not need a fresh declaration to impose the tax.

issues.legal_issue: A tax on minerals need not be shown to fund mine regulation or mineral development, and need not have a quid pro quo.
material_facts: The challenged levy was a tax or cess, not a fee.
The challenge asserted that the levy was invalid without proof that its proceeds were required for regulating mines or developing minerals.
issues.conclusion: The levy did not need to be justified by a specific regulatory purpose or by proof of a quid pro quo.
issues.legal_principle: Taxes augment the general revenues of the State and need not be raised for a particular purpose or service. The Court distinguished taxes from fees and noted that quid pro quo is irrelevant to regulatory fees. It relied on Corporation of Calcutta v. Liberty Cinema.

predicates.mineral_levy_challenge: The proceeding challenges a levy imposed on minerals.
predicates.levy_is_tax_not_fee: The levy raises public revenue as a tax rather than charging for a particular service as a fee.

issues.definition: When a challenged mineral levy is a tax rather than a fee, its validity does not depend on proof of a particular regulatory use or a quid pro quo.

issues.legal_issue: A law that imposes a levy only for a defined past period is not thereby a temporary statute that expires at the end of that period.
material_facts: The validation law was enacted after the period for which it made the levies operative.
The law contained no provision stating that the statute itself expired on a particular date.
The specified end date limited the period of the levy, not the life of the statute.
issues.conclusion: The validation law was not a temporary statute and had not expired when the levy period ended.
issues.legal_principle: A temporary statute is one that expires after a specified duration. The duration of a levy and the life of the enactment creating it are distinct. The Court relied on Maganti Subrahmanyam v. State of Andhra Pradesh and Madurai District Central Cooperative Bank Ltd. v. Third Income-Tax Officer, Madurai.

predicates.statute_validity_challenge: The proceeding challenges the continuing operation or validity of an enactment.
predicates.levy_limited_to_past_period: The enactment makes the levy operative only for a defined past period.
predicates.statute_has_no_expiry_term: The enactment does not provide that the statute itself expires at the end of that period.

issues.definition: A defined period for which a levy applies does not cause the enactment itself to expire when it contains no separate expiry term.

issues.legal_issue: The machinery for collecting and refunding a retrospectively validated levy remains available after the period for which the levy applied.
material_facts: The validation law created a levy for a defined past period.
The law also preserved a right to claim a refund of amounts paid in excess of what was due.
Some valid amounts remained uncollected, while some amounts might have been collected in excess.
issues.conclusion: The machinery necessary to collect unpaid amounts and to process claims for excess payments remained available after the levy period ended.
issues.legal_principle: The provision allowing claims for refunds of excess payments presupposes that the relevant machinery remains operative after the levy period. The Court found no basis to keep that machinery alive only for refunds and not for collection of valid, unpaid amounts.

predicates.validation_statute_challenge: The proceeding challenges a law enacted to validate a levy previously held invalid by a court.
predicates.retrospective_levy_created: The law creates the levy for a past period by giving legal effect to the levy terms for that period.
predicates.law_preserves_excess_payment_claims: The law allows a person to claim a refund of payments exceeding the amount due.

issues.definition: When a law retrospectively creates a levy and preserves claims for excess payments, the machinery for dealing with those claims also remains available for collection and refund.

issues.legal_issue: Overlapping provisions validating mineral cesses do not authorize charging the same mineral quantity twice where the State undertakes that only one levy will be imposed.
material_facts: Two provisions relating to mineral cess in one State were included among the provisions validated by the law.
It was apprehended that both provisions might result in a charge on the same mineral quantity.
The State expressly stated that there would be only one levy for a given year or quantity removed.
issues.conclusion: The Court accepted the State’s assurance that there would not be a double levy and that only one levy would apply to a given year or quantity removed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court resolved the specific apprehension by relying on the State’s clear assurance that the overlapping provisions would not result in a double charge.

predicates.validation_statute_challenge: The proceeding challenges a law enacted to validate a levy previously held invalid by a court.
predicates.overlapping_levy_provisions: More than one validated provision could appear to impose a levy on the same mineral quantity or period.
predicates.state_assures_single_charge: The State clearly assures the court that it will impose only one levy on the relevant quantity or period.

issues.definition: When overlapping validated provisions raise a risk of duplicate charges and the State assures a single charge, the same mineral quantity is charged only once.
